title: Remembering without hatred
hook: the Ardas names martyrs, not enemies; memory is for courage, not revenge

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rattan Singh Bhangu, the chronicler who set the hard century down in verse so the Sikh side would be told. Today, what Sikhs do with all that memory.

Partway through the Ardas, the prayer said standing at the close of Sikh gatherings, comes a passage that's hard to hear. It remembers Sikhs cut limb from limb, scalped, broken on the wheel, sawn apart, who gave their heads and kept their faith. The congregation stands with folded hands and answers Waheguru. And something is missing. The governors, the generals, the invaders who did these things: their names aren't there. Today: remembering without hatred.
screen: `THE ARDAS REMEMBERS THE MARTYRS.` → `CUT, SCALPED, BROKEN, SAWN.` → `AND NOT ONE ENEMY IS NAMED.`

segments.voice: Start with what the prayer keeps. The Ardas names the Gurus, the Sahibzade, the Panj Piare, and then the ones whose names are lost, by what they endured and what they held on to: their hair, their faith, their Guru. Memory pointed at the ones who stood, not the ones who struck. Second, a line Guru Arjan left in the Guru Granth Sahib, here in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. It comes from a Guru who was himself put to death, and it can be heard alongside the long list of martyrs. It doesn't say nothing bad happened. It says the heart doesn't have to be organized around the people who did it. Third, how the prayer ends. After all that suffering, the Ardas asks for sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Everyone, not everyone except them. A few weeks back, this path met a minister whose grief turned into a slaughter; Sikhs tell that story too. Read this way, the Ardas keeps grief from being handed on as hatred. When Sikhs stand and remember, the prayer doesn't ask who to pay back. It asks, in effect, could I stand like that? Courage, not revenge.
screen: `THE PRAYER NAMES THOSE WHO STOOD.` · `NO ONE IS MY ENEMY, NO ONE A STRANGER.` · `IT ENDS ASKING THE GOOD OF ALL.` · `HATRED IS NOT HANDED ON.` · then, large: `COURAGE, NOT REVENGE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who went through something hard, in your family or your own life, and see it plainly. If your attention drifts to the one who caused it, bring it gently back to the one who endured: what did they hold on to? If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out; if not, let any anger pass like weather.
Ardas, the prayer said standing at the close of Sikh gatherings. It names the martyrs by what they endured, names no enemy, and ends asking the good of all. Today's word.
Your line: courage, not revenge. The prayer remembers who stood. That's day eight hundred seventy-seven.

chat.says: I heard Sikhs pray about their martyrs. Do they name the people who killed them?
options: No. The Ardas remembers what the martyrs endured, names no enemy, and ends asking the good of all.
Yes, the Ardas lists the persecutors by name so that nobody ever forgets what they did.
No, the Ardas skips the martyrs completely, so that nobody has to remember the suffering.
